text:
Chapter Fourteen


Outside, the late sun had turned the sky to rust. There was a temporary reprieve from the day’s mist, with streaks of blue visible between the bands of clouds. The unseasonable chill went all the way down to the bone, and it felt more like March than early June. Maggie was glad for the chunky cardigan she had thrown over her T-shirt before leaving Hawthorn. She pulled it tight across her chest as she stood beneath Bean There’s awning. She had errands to run and little daylight left to complete them, but Taliesin didn’t make a move to leave first and neither did she.


“Artie, huh?”


Taliesin cringed. “Please don’t call me that.”


“It’s weird to think you aren’t famous to everyone. You mean the whole world isn’t gossiping about why the great Arthur Taliesin left the hallowed halls of Dartwood for Hawthorn?”


“People gossip about me?” His eyebrows drew together in a furrow, and Maggie’s fingers itched to soothe it away. Before she could explain what she’d meant, Arthur shook his head and went on. “My brother’s high school friends definitely don’t care about my job. To them, I’m just Rory’s weird older brother he sometimes dragged to house parties. Even if they know who Arthur Taliesin is, I’m not sure they would have ever made the connection.” He shrugged. “When you meet Rory, you’ll get it. He’s very cool.”


When you meet Rory. Maggie couldn’t really envision a scenario where she would need to meet his younger brother, but she gave Taliesin a friendly smile anyway. “You’re very cool in certain circles,” she said.


“Small ones, maybe.” He let out another one of those laughs that was more like a huff. She wondered, briefly, what it would feel like to make him really laugh.


“You know…” Taliesin began, pausing as if hunting for the words he wanted to say. “It’s a relief that I’m not doing this alone anymore.”


Before she could stop herself, Maggie said, “Why did you ever assume you could?”


Instead of the anger or annoyance she expected, which she maybe wanted to tease out of him, he smirked before his expression turned soft, the light catching his glasses. “You’re right, of course.”


They seemed to have drawn together, slowly, over the course of this conversation, until there was just a breath between their fingers at their sides.


Maggie couldn’t be sure who pulled away first, but then she was fiddling with her hair tie and Taliesin was stuffing his hand in his pocket and asking her where she parked. “I walked,” she said as she finished twisting the elastic around her bun.


Taliesin tensed beside her. “You did what?”


“I put one foot in front of the other until I arrived here.”


“In the rain?”


She reached into her tote bag and pulled out her sage-green umbrella, dotted with runes that deflected water, but that didn’t seem to make him feel any better.


“Maggie,” he said, frustration curling the edges of his words, “you were attacked by a ghoul in town twelve days ago.”


She ticked off days on her fingers. “Thirteen.” His expression had turned from soft to sour so fast, Maggie wanted to laugh. “What? There hasn’t been a banshee sighted in town yet. And obviously I can handle myself against a ghoul.” She reached into the neck of her T-shirt and pulled out the charm she’d thrown on before she left. It was a circular piece of hawthorn, the wood grain polished and shining, with a protection rune calibrated to her birthday carved into it. “I’m being careful.”


“Maggie. It’s irresponsible.”


There was only the hint of pleasure at the way he said her name through his clenched teeth before annoyance set in, and she barely suppressed the roll of her eyes. Taliesin seemed to have a real gift for reminding her that he was nothing more than an annoying, paternalistic know-it-all. Now if only the rest of her body could get the memo, because it seemed to be heating up in pleasure at his concern.


“Now who’s lecturing,” she said under her breath.


“I’m walking you home.” It wasn’t a suggestion or a request, and before Maggie could even begin to protest, he turned in the direction of Hawthorn and started walking. The top of the tree and the tallest spire of Ilex Hall were just visible in the distance.


Maggie sighed. By the time she went after him, he was already halfway down the block, moving in long strides as if determined to get her home as fast as possible. She needed to practically speed walk to catch up with him. It was undignified. “Wait! If you insist on walking me home, you’re going to have to run my errands with me.”


He looked back at her with narrowed eyes. “I have time.”


She knew he didn’t. He needed to get on the road back to Atlantia, back to his nephew and brother and father, but for some reason he didn’t even trust her to walk through her own neighborhood back to her apartment.


“It’s your time to waste, I guess.” She stuffed her fists into her sweater pockets as they walked in silence. At the corner, Arthur stopped abruptly and turned on his heel to face her.


His cheeks were red with the chill. “Getting you home safe isn’t a waste of my time.”


“Oh.” Maggie bit her lip as awkward tension bloomed between them. She was desperate to defuse it, but instead only managed to mutter a quiet “Thanks.” She gestured across the street toward the other corner. “Um. Glinda’s is right there.”


Crystals hung in the shop windows, catching the evening light, and inside, Glinda’s shop cat, Mustard, curled on his toadstool-shaped bed. The royal-purple door was dotted with flyers for events around Galloway—gardening magic classes at the greenhouses, a weekly crochet circle at Bean There, and an old, curling flyer for the Beltane festival on Brig Beach.


Maggie pressed her palm to the door, but before she could open it, Taliesin asked her worriedly, “Did my students already eat all of the candy I replaced?”


“Oh, gods above, no. Dahlia’s birthday is in a few weeks. I’m just picking up her present.”


The bell chimed delicately with their arrival, and there was the ghost of a touch low on her back as Taliesin led her into the shop. But before she could turn, the touch was gone, and Taliesin was already escaping down one of the aisles to look at something intently.


“Hey, Dr. Linden!” called the student behind the counter, Nat. “Oh, and Dr. Taliesin, too!”


From somewhere in the shop, Taliesin responded with a warm “Evening, Nat,” but Maggie was suddenly nervous.


“Dr. Taliesin and I were working late on a project,” Maggie explained, answering a question that no one in the shop had asked. I need to get a grip. Nat didn’t care that she was here with Taliesin. They had already returned to the alchemy textbook they had spread out on the counter, a pencil in their hand as they worked through a problem set to prepare for their upcoming final.


In the window, Mustard stretched on his toadstool and yawned as Taliesin walked by and reached out a hand to scratch between the cat’s ears. The cat purred contentedly and then curled back into his tight ball while Taliesin returned to browsing. Glass jars filled with tiny, jeweled sweets lined one wall, the flavors ranging from Maggie’s favorite lavender to the new chamomile to tart raspberry. Along another wall, there was a range of decoction powders in delicate cotton bags with drawstrings. A new display on the counter held small hourglasses full of glittering sand. Maggie sighed. She wished she had hours to spend combing Glinda’s, but Taliesin’s towering presence over the squat, uneven shelves reminded her that she should come back another time, so she went straight to the counter.


“What can I get you?” Nat asked, tucking a pencil in their textbook to save their spot.


“Glinda sent me an email this afternoon saying my order was ready for pickup?” Never mind that the email had also included a paragraph about the handsome professor who came in earlier that week asking for recommendations for candies to bring her. No, no one else needed to know about that.


“Give me a sec,” Nat said before disappearing into the stockroom.


As she waited, Taliesin appeared beside her, his hands full of little boxes that he set down on the counter. One toppled over, and they both crouched down to pick it up, their fingers brushing as they reached for it. Maggie pulled back. As Taliesin grabbed the box, she caught a glimpse of the tiny toy train inside.


“For my nephew,” he explained. “He found an old train track set of mine in my dad’s house, but we couldn’t find the train that went with it. I’ve been on the lookout for ones that will fit the tracks. Lucky we were here.”


Nat reappeared, carrying a small, hinged box. They set it on top of their textbook and opened it, revealing a delicate pair of earrings made of gilded wire. The earrings were twisted into precise runes and decorated with tiny drops of crystal that would sit so well against Dahlia’s dark hair. Nestled in the bottom of the box was a small card with the incantation that activated the wired runes.


Over her shoulder, Taliesin admired them. “What’s the spell?”


“A memory spell,” Maggie said. “It just makes memories a little sharper. Dahlia’s always complaining about being scatterbrained and forgetting important things.”


Maggie had ordered the gift long before Beltane, before a memory spell had wreaked havoc on her own life. She wondered now if she’d been wearing something similar that day, whether the two magics would have canceled each other out. Would she have ever kissed TK if she’d been so sure she’d remember him the next day? Normally, Maggie was careful, and careful meant not letting anyone in who might mess up the delicate balance of her life in Galloway.


And then there was Taliesin and this bargain between them. Ostensibly she’d entered it to get her office back, to get her life back on track, but she had a sinking feeling every time she felt the strange pull between them that she had, instead, veered farther off course. She looked over her shoulder, trying to catch a glimpse of Taliesin, and found him already watching her, his gaze sharp and searching. What had he seen pass across her features? She snapped the jewelry box shut.


“Thanks, Nat,” Maggie said as they packaged the box in a gift bag.


After Nat handed her the bag, she wanted to vanish, to escape out the door and return to the street, lest Nat think she was waiting for Taliesin as they rang up the trains he’d bought for his nephew. Instead, she busied herself with scratching Mustard’s ears until the creature purred.


“We’ll let you get back to studying,” she heard him say. It was so easy for him to say we so casually. As if he didn’t care whether Nat did gossip about them. Maybe he didn’t. Maybe it never occurred to him what could happen if people thought they were together. “Good luck on your exams!”


When they were outside, Maggie looked back through the shop window, but Nat had already returned to their textbook, wholly uninterested in what Maggie and Taliesin were doing out in Galloway on a Thursday night. “I got you something,” Taliesin said, interrupting her thoughts, his hand outstretched toward her.


She frowned but took the cellophane-wrapped candy from Taliesin’s palm. Before she unwrapped it, she glanced up at him. “I thought you might like it,” he explained, though she hadn’t asked.


She unwrapped the sweet and plopped it in her mouth. A sugary floral burst of honeysuckle bloomed on her tongue. She had never tasted this flavor of Glinda’s, but something tugged on her memory, though she couldn’t quite place it. She didn’t understand how this man could infuriate her one moment and charm her the next. It was confusing, and she was sure her confusion was plain on her face.


“Where next?” Taliesin asked, casting a nervous glance at the sky.


“Willoughby’s. They ordered in a rare edition of Branagh’s Aubade for me.”


They walked side by side, their bags knocking into each other occasionally, but they were quiet, both lost in their own thoughts. Though they were the only ones on the street, music still poured out of Rodrigo’s, where Thursday Open Mic Night was apparently still on. An off-key serenade echoed against the old brick buildings, when suddenly Taliesin tensed and, without warning, reached his hand out to stop Maggie from walking on.


He peered into the darkness of the alley between buildings and said, in a hush, “What was that?”


Maggie looked down at where his hand grazed her stomach. “I didn’t hear—” But then Maggie did hear it. It was somewhere beneath the music coming from Rodrigo’s, something guttural and deep. A hum that didn’t quite sound like it came from earthside. Maggie was sure that if the air didn’t already carry an unseasonable chill from the pall, they would have felt the presence—whatever it was—like a breeze slipping from the alleyway’s darkness. Maggie’s heartbeat sped up, and sweat broke out on her brow as she remembered the ghoul, with its horrible teeth and spiderweb hair, its mindless hunt. The hollow look in its eyes as she banished it to wherever it came from.


It was instinct that made her reach out her hand and grab Taliesin’s arm, the one that was already shielding her from whatever was in the alley. It must have been instinct, for him, too, that made him step in front of her. It all happened so quickly, their movement toward each other as easy as breathing.


She waited for a ghoul to drag itself out of the alley, for a banshee to swoop down from one of the building’s eves and screech into the night, but all she saw was a wispy shadow. Her pulse calmed.


“It’s just a wraith,” Taliesin confirmed, his shoulder sagging.


The wraith was otherworldly, slow and fast all at once, appearing to jump from shadow to shadow without moving between them. Sometimes there was the suggestion of the human it might have been—the curve of a shoulder, the nod of a head—but mostly it was incorporeal and indistinct, fuzzy-edged. Maggie shuddered.


Wraiths were the least dangerous of the fantasmia. They couldn’t grab or bite or poison. They didn’t possess ethereal screams that could maim. The worst a wraith could do was drop the temperature in a room a few degrees or run through a person, leaving them shivering and maybe a little frostbitten. Near a fountain of energy like a pall, they often took on more human shapes. They were the source of most childhood ghost stories, of tall slender men standing at the foots of beds or lonely women sweeping down hallways, but they were relatively harmless.


Wraiths were something of a mystery. No one knew if they were human souls or something else meant to mimic human shapes, and that uncertainty had always made Maggie uncomfortable and more than a little existential.


“I’d rather a wraith than a ghoul or a banshee,” Taliesin said. “But maybe we should cross the street.”


“Sure,” Maggie said, staring down into the alley as the wraith seemed to watch where they stood on the corner.


Taliesin cleared his throat, and Maggie pulled her eyes away from the wraith. He glanced down at his arm where she was still holding him tight. Heat spread up from her neck, and she released him, sure he’d have pinprick indents where her nails had dug in.


“Sorry,” she mumbled.


“Don’t be.” He said it quickly and so quietly that she wasn’t sure she’d heard him correctly.


They left the wraith behind them. When they reached Willoughby’s, halfway down the block, both of them turned to see the wraith still following them. It slinked alongside the brick of the buildings, sticking to the shadows. When Taliesin reached behind him and opened Willoughby’s door, the wraith vanished, returning to the shadows it had come from. Maggie was unsettled by the wraith, by the way it seemed to stalk them down the street. Maybe Taliesin was right and walking downtown had been a bad idea after all, but if nothing else, Maggie was a stubborn creature. Together, they walked into the inviting warmth and bright light of Willoughby’s Books.
